context: A bank savings account pays simple interest at a whole-number percentage per annum. The amount wanted after a given number of years is given in rand, and the amount to invest now is asked for, correct to the cent.

params.why: the principal is not already a whole number of rand, so the rounding step is real
the principal never lies exactly half a cent from a cent, so the rounding is unambiguous

stem: A bank offers a savings account which pays simple interest at a rate of ${=r}$ % per annum. If you want to accumulate $\text{R{=A}}$ in ${=n}$ years, how much should you invest now? Give your answer in rand, correct to two decimal places.
solution: Read the question carefully and write down the given information: $\begin{aligned}A&=\text{R{=A}}\\P&=?\\i&=\frac{{=r}}{100}=0.0{=r}\\n&={=n}\end{aligned}$
Write down the simple interest formula: $A=P(1+in)$
Substitute the given values and work out the bracket: $\begin{aligned}\text{R{=A}}&=P\left(1+0.0{=r}\times{=n}\right)\\\text{R{=A}}&=P\times{=ds}\end{aligned}$
Divide both sides by ${=ds}$ to find $P$: $P=\frac{\text{R{=A}}}{{=ds}}$
Calculate and round to two decimal places: $P=\text{R{=fixed(P, 2)}}$
notes: The book's typical exercise, a direct parametrisation of ex9-1-6 (R15000, 6 %, 5 years gives R11538.46 when r = 6, n = 5, k = 30). Not one of the listed gaps; added because the bank holds only two standard items for this objective. The requires keep P a non-integer and away from an exact half-cent tie (a tie occurs only when 20000A/d is an odd integer), so every instance rounds the same way for any solver. Rate is a single-digit whole percent. Numeric family, so no distractors and no misconception ids.
